case.title: Best-improved supplier, worst-performing valve
case.setting: Brenmoor Heat Systems (fictional) builds AH-series air-source heat pumps, about 4,100 units a month. In January 2026 it launched SupplierPath, a supplier-quality programme that scores suppliers each quarter and grants dock-to-stock status (no receiving inspection) at a score of 85 or more. The VA-220 four-way reversing valve comes from Pellacott Precision (about 80% of volume) and Durrant-Hale Components (20%). Pellacott's score rose from 70 to 89 and it reached dock-to-stock in July 2026. Over the same period, field claims coded to the VA-220 rose sharply. Brenmoor also onboarded 14 new installer firms in early 2026 and rolled out controller firmware 4.2 in March.
case.presentingRequest: The COO asks: why have VA-220 field failures risen while Pellacott's SupplierPath score improved, and what should Brenmoor do now, including about the six Pellacott lots receiving has on hold?

initialEvidence.source: Email from Marcus Ilvane, VP Operations, to quality leadership, 12 Oct 2026
initialEvidence.text: Subject: VA-220 claims. Let's not chase the wrong rabbit. Pellacott is our best-improved supplier: SupplierPath score 70 to 89, dock-to-stock since July, every lot certified 100% leak-tested. What changed on our side this year is 14 new installer firms and firmware 4.2. Field service already tells me the new firms' jobs are where the failures are. Receiving put six Pellacott lots on hold on 1 October, and that means a line stoppage next week. Pellacott has offered fresh certificates for those lots; once they arrive, release them. I want an installer remediation plan by Friday.

catalogue.text: Rig LT-04 found disconnected and tagged 'OUT OF SERVICE – pressure transducer failed 9 Jan 2026'. LT-04 controller memory: last test cycle 18 Dec 2025. actions.text: Quarantine all 2026-built Pellacott VA-220 stock (including the six held lots), suspend Pellacott's dock-to-stock status, and release VA-220 stock only after Brenmoor-run helium leak testing.
Suspend the certification of the 14 installer firms onboarded in 2026 and charge their VA-220 warranty claims back to them.
Release the six held VA-220 lots to production once Pellacott supplies fresh certificates of conformance for them.

Change SupplierPath scoring so that submitted test records earn credit only when backed by rig logs or a witnessed test, starting from the next audit cycle.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: From 12 January 2026 Pellacott built VA-220 valves with a new Corlin seal on a new Line 3. Its only VA-220 leak rig, LT-04, had failed on 9 January and logged no test after 18 December 2025. Rather than stop shipments, Pellacott issued 2026 certificates citing LT-04 with per-piece values copied from November 2025 tables. Because these fabricated records were complete and showed 100% pass, Pellacott's SupplierPath test-record component rose from 58 to 100. That rise lifted its score from 70 to 89 and triggered automatic dock-to-stock, which removed Brenmoor's last receiving check. Brenmoor's own helium retest found 11% of never-installed 2026-built Pellacott valves leaking at the seat, against about 1% of 2025-built and none of Durrant-Hale's. Teardowns of returned valves show the same seat defect with braze joints intact. Claim rates are the same for legacy and new installers and for firmware 4.1 and 4.2, and they stay at baseline whenever Durrant-Hale valves are fitted. The new-installer pattern seen by field service is confounded by build year. Whether the seal compound or Line 3 assembly creates the defect cannot be separated. Whether other suppliers' records are also unreal is open. The right step is containment, with Brenmoor running its own tests.

answers.rationale: C5 shows nearly identical claim rates for legacy (41) and new (42) installers on Pellacott 2026 valves. It shows baseline rates (5–7) in every installer group with Durrant-Hale valves, braze joints intact on all returns, and seat leaks in never-installed stock. The pattern field service sees in E5 comes from new firms installing 2026-built units.

C5 establishes that 2026-built Pellacott valves are defective before installation (11% seat leaks in unpowered stock against about 1% for 2025-built). C10 shows the cited rig LT-04 was out of service all of 2026, no other rig ran VA-220, and every checked 2026 per-piece table is a copy of a 2025 sequence. So the certificates do not reflect real tests.

H3 needs the recorded tests to have been performed. C10 shows LT-04 logged no cycle after 18 Dec 2025, no other equipment could test VA-220, and the values were recycled. The tests were not done as recorded. C5 alone leaves H3 open because it did not replicate the pressure-decay method.

In C5, units on firmware 4.1 (40) and 4.2 (42) fail at the same rate with Pellacott 2026 valves. Durrant-Hale valves stay at baseline under 4.2, and never-powered warehouse valves already leak. The firmware timing is coincidental.

E3 and C8 show test-record scores rising across the programme under the same unverified scoring incentive, so the claim is live. But no evidence checks any other supplier's rig logs or raw data, and no catalogue item settles it either way.

C5 gives the mechanism: the returned valves' seat leak matches the dominant claim code in E2. It shows the defect is present before installation and covaries with valve source and build year. It also rules out the main rivals (installers and firmware) by stratification.
C5 shows that installer cohort makes no difference to failure rates for a given valve source, and that installation damage (braze joints) is absent. This is evidence against the link itself.
Units left on 4.1 because they lack a connectivity module fail at the same rate as 4.2 units, and 4.2 units with Durrant-Hale valves stay at baseline. This counts directly against the firmware link.

The seal change coincides with the defect onset (E4), and the defect sits in the slide seal (C5). But C5 states that the seal compound was not analysed and that the Corlin seal and the Line 3 assembly change are fully confounded. Causation by the seal source is therefore not established.

E3 gives the scoring formula. The test-record component, weighted 0.40, rose from 58 to 100, adding about 17 of the 19-point rise, while the other components moved only a few points. The link is mechanical.

With 11% of 2026-built Pellacott stock leaking and Pellacott's records shown not to be genuine, the best next action is to contain the stock and test it independently. This does not depend on whether the seal or Line 3 is to blame.

Installers are shown not to drive failures. Suspending them and charging claims back punishes the wrong party, cuts installation capacity and leaves the defective parts in place. No live rival hypothesis would make this action beneficial.

C10 shows Pellacott's certificates are fabricated, and Pellacott has no working VA-220 rig to produce fresh ones. Releasing the lots on that paper would undo the only protective hold and ship stock that C5 shows is about 11% defective.

If the Corlin seal were confirmed as the cause, reverting to Ferrand (still an approved source, E4) would clearly help, and reverting costs little if it is wrong. But C5 cannot separate the seal from the Line 3 change, so committing now is not justified.

The scoring flaw is confirmed: E3 shows unverified self-reported records drove the score, and C10 shows those records were fabricated. Requiring verification is reasonable, but it takes effect next cycle and does nothing about defective stock now, so it is not among the best next actions.

The highest-ranked substantive action (A1) needs only two things: that 2026-built Pellacott stock is defective before installation (C5) and that Pellacott's certificates cannot be trusted (C10). Both are established. The open questions about the seal and other suppliers do not affect it.

truth.authoringNotes: The initial file points three ways: installers (VP, field service), firmware (field service) and the supplier (change notice, claim code). Pellacott's high audit score acts as a credibility trap. E6 quietly names rig LT-04, and E3 shows suspiciously perfect records after poor 2025 paperwork. C5 alone settles the defect, installer and firmware items, but leaves fabrication against honest test escape open because it did not replicate Pellacott's method. C10 alone settles fabrication (H3 contradicted) but not whether the defect predates installation or the installer and firmware rivals. C3, C13 and C9 hint at gaming (unwitnessed tests, a rebate incentive) but settle nothing. C2 and C6 keep the firmware and installer rivals alive without settling them. H5 stays unknown because no item examines other suppliers' raw data. A4 is premature because seal source and Line 3 are confounded in every 2026 sample.
